da-2024-da-17.approach: z-score normalisation uses only the mean and the standard deviation: $z = \dfrac{v-\mu}{\sigma}$. The minimum and maximum are decoys (they belong to min–max normalisation).
da-2024-da-17.given:
| quantity | value |
|---|---|
| min, max | ₹46000, ₹170000 (not needed) |
| mean $\mu$ | ₹96000 |
| std. dev. $\sigma$ | ₹21000 |
| value $v$ | ₹106000 |

steps.title: Pick the right formula
steps.body:
z-score normalisation measures how many standard deviations a value lies from the mean:

$$z = \frac{v-\mu}{\sigma}.$$

Only $\mu$ and $\sigma$ appear, so the given minimum and maximum play no role.

steps.title: Substitute the numbers
steps.body:
$$z = \frac{106000-96000}{21000} = \frac{10000}{21000} = \frac{10}{21} \approx 0.476.$$

So ₹106000 lies about half a standard deviation above the mean.

optionAnalysis.reason: $0.217 \approx \frac{10000}{46000}$: dividing the deviation by the **minimum** instead of the standard deviation.
$0.623 \approx \frac{106000}{170000}$: dividing the value by the **maximum** (a crude max-scaling), not standardising.
$2.304 \approx \frac{106000}{46000}$: dividing the value by the **minimum** — meaningless as a normalisation.

da-2024-da-17.shortcut: $\frac{10}{21}$ is a little under $\frac12$ — only (B) fits.
pitfalls: Using min–max normalisation $\frac{v-\min}{\max-\min} = \frac{60000}{124000} \approx 0.484$ — a different method (it happens to be near 0.476, but the question asks for the z-score).
Forgetting to subtract the mean before dividing by σ.

da-2024-da-18.approach: Check each pair against the reason reconstruction can fail. Inorder + (pre or post) always works; preorder + postorder fails for general trees only because a node with a **single** child cannot be placed left or right — and a full binary tree has no such node. Inorder alone never fixes the root.

steps.title: (i) Preorder + (ii) Inorder: unique
steps.body: The first preorder key is the root. Finding it in the inorder sequence splits the remaining keys into the left subtree (keys before it) and the right subtree (keys after it), and the sizes tell how to split the rest of the preorder. Recursing rebuilds **any** binary tree with distinct keys uniquely, so (A) is sufficient.

steps.title: (ii) Inorder + (iii) Postorder: unique
steps.body: Same argument with the root taken as the **last** postorder key: the inorder position of the root separates left and right subtrees, and recursion is forced. So (B) is sufficient.

steps.title: (i) Preorder + (iii) Postorder: unique for full trees
steps.body:
For a general binary tree, a node with one child gives the same pre- and postorder whether the child is left or right — that is the only ambiguity.

In a **full** binary tree each internal node has exactly two children. Then, after the root $r$, the next preorder key $\ell$ must be the root of the **left** subtree. In postorder, every key up to and including $\ell$ forms the left subtree; the keys after $\ell$ (before $r$) form the right subtree. Both pieces are again full trees, so recursion is forced. Hence (C) is sufficient.

steps.title: (ii) Inorder alone: not unique
steps.body: The two full binary trees in the figure both have inorder $D\,B\,E\,A\,C$ but different roots (their preorders are $A\,B\,D\,E\,C$ and $B\,D\,A\,E\,C$). One inorder sequence cannot tell them apart, so (D) is **not** sufficient.

scene.caption: Same inorder D B E A C — two different full binary trees

answer.value: **(A), (B) and (C)** — any two of the three traversals suffice for a full binary tree; inorder alone does not

optionAnalysis.reason: Preorder gives the root, inorder splits left/right — unique for every binary tree.
Postorder gives the root (last key), inorder splits left/right — unique for every binary tree.
In a full binary tree no node has a single child, so the key after the root in preorder is the left child and its position in postorder splits the subtrees — unique.
Inorder alone does not identify the root; the two trees in the figure share inorder D B E A C.

da-2024-da-18.shortcut: Memorise: pre+in and post+in always work; pre+post works exactly when no node has one child (full trees); a single traversal never works.
pitfalls: Rejecting (C) by recalling "pre + post is not enough" — that holds for general binary trees, not full ones.
Assuming keys may repeat; reconstruction assumes distinct node labels.
da-2024-da-18.verification: For the pair of trees in the figure: preorders differ ($ABDEC$ vs $BDAEC$) and postorders differ ($DEBCA$ vs $DECAB$), so any pair containing pre or post separates them, while inorder alone does not.

da-2024-da-19.approach: An implication $P \implies Q$ can fail only on rows where $P$ is true. Each premise here ($\neg x \land y$ or $x \land \neg y$) is true on exactly **one** row, so each option needs a single row check.

steps.title: Where the premises are true
steps.body: $\neg x \land y$ is true only for $x=0, y=1$; $x \land \neg y$ is true only for $x=1, y=0$. On every other row the implication is true automatically (false premise).

steps.title: (A) fails at x = 0, y = 1
steps.body: Conclusion $y \implies x$ becomes $1 \implies 0 = \text{F}$. Premise true, conclusion false, so (A) is **false** on that row — not a tautology.

steps.title: (B) and (D) at x = 1, y = 0
steps.body:
(B): $\neg x \implies y$ is $0 \implies 0 = \text{T}$.

(D): $y \implies x$ is $0 \implies 1 = \text{T}$.

Both are true on their only critical row, so (B) and (D) are tautologies.

steps.title: (C) at x = 0, y = 1
steps.body:
$
eg x \implies y$ is $1 \implies 1 = 	ext{T}$, so (C) is a tautology. In fact its premise $
eg x \land y$ makes both $
eg x$ and $y$ true.

answer.value: **(B), (C), (D)** are tautologies; (A) is false at $x=0, y=1$

optionAnalysis.reason: At $x=0, y=1$: premise $\neg x \land y = 1$, conclusion $y \implies x = 1 \implies 0 = 0$ — false, so not a tautology.
Only critical row $x=1, y=0$: $\neg x \implies y = 0 \implies 0 = 1$ — always true.
Only critical row $x=0, y=1$: $\neg x \implies y = 1 \implies 1 = 1$ — always true.
Only critical row $x=1, y=0$: $y \implies x = 0 \implies 1 = 1$ — always true.

da-2024-da-19.shortcut: (B) and (D) have a false antecedent ($\neg x$ or $y$ is 0) inside the conclusion whenever the premise holds, so the conclusion is vacuously true; (C)'s premise literally contains $\neg x$ and $y$.
pitfalls: Reading $p \implies q$ as false whenever $p$ is false — it is **true** then.
Treating this as single-answer: it is a multiple-select question.

da-2024-da-20.approach: Trace the last-element-pivot (Lomuto) partition on the already sorted input: every element is $\le$ the pivot, so the "swap" index $i$ always equals the scan index $j$ and the pivot already sits at its final place. Nothing ever moves, so an implementation that skips self-swaps does **0** swaps — the minimum.

steps.title: Partition 1: pivot 100
steps.body: Scan $60, 70, 80, 90$: each is $\le 100$, so $i$ advances with $j$ and every exchange would be $A[i] \leftrightarrow A[i]$ (same position). The pivot's final index is $i+1 = 4$, its current index. **No element moves.** Split: $[60, 70, 80, 90]$ | $100$ | $[\,]$.

steps.title: Partitions on 4, 3, 2 elements
steps.body: Pivot $90$ on $[60,70,80,90]$, then $80$ on $[60,70,80]$, then $70$ on $[60,70]$: the same thing happens each time — every scanned element is smaller than the pivot, the pivot is already last. The single element $[60]$ needs no work.

steps.title: Count the swaps
steps.body:
In every call, each would-be swap exchanges an element with itself, which changes nothing and is skipped by a swap-only-when-needed implementation (`if i != j`). Since the array is already sorted and no element ever has to change position, the minimum number of swaps is

$$\mathbf{0}.$$

(The comparisons are still the worst case: $4+3+2+1 = 10$.)

da-2024-da-20.shortcut: An already sorted array with last-element pivot: every element is already in its final place, so no swap is ever *required* — the minimum is 0.
pitfalls: Counting textbook Lomuto's self-swaps: $(4+1)+(3+1)+(2+1)+(1+1) = 14$ "swaps" that move nothing — the question asks for the **minimum**.
Confusing swaps with comparisons (10 here — sorted input is the worst case for comparisons, not swaps).
da-2024-da-20.verification: Hoare-style partitioning with the last element as pivot reaches the same conclusion: the left scan finds no element $>$ pivot before the pivot itself, so no out-of-place pair exists in any call — 0 exchanges.

da-2024-da-25.approach: Factor $M^2 + 12M = M(M + 12I)$, so $\det = \det M \cdot \det(M+12I)$. Row 3 of $M$ equals row 1 + row 2, hence $\det M = 0$ and the whole determinant is 0 — no need to form $M^2$.

steps.title: Factor the matrix polynomial
steps.body:
$M^2 + 12M = M\,M + M\,(12I) = M\,(M + 12I)$, and $\det(AB) = \det A \cdot \det B$, so

$$\det(M^2+12M) = \det M \cdot \det(M+12I).$$

steps.title: Spot the dependent row
steps.body: Row 1 + Row 2 $= (1+3,\ 2+1,\ 3+3) = (4, 3, 6) =$ Row 3. A matrix with linearly dependent rows is singular: $\det M = 0$.

steps.title: Conclude
steps.body: $\det(M^2+12M) = 0 \times \det(M+12I) = \mathbf{0}$, whatever $\det(M+12I)$ is.

da-2024-da-25.shortcut: Any polynomial $p(M)$ with zero constant term has $M$ as a factor, so $\det p(M) = 0$ whenever $M$ is singular.
pitfalls: Expanding $M^2 + 12M$ entry by entry — long and error-prone.
Thinking $\det(A+B) = \det A + \det B$ (false in general).

da-2024-da-26.approach: First-step analysis on a 3-state Markov chain (no current even streak / one even just seen / done) with $p = P(\text{even}) = \frac12$; two linear equations give the expected number of throws.

steps.title: Set up the states
steps.body: Let $E_0$ = expected further throws when the streak of evens is 0 (start, or last throw odd), and $E_1$ = expected further throws when the last throw was even (streak 1). The target is $E_0$.

steps.title: Write the first-step equations
steps.body:
From streak 0: one throw, then even (prob $\frac12$) → streak 1, odd → streak 0:
$$E_0 = 1 + \tfrac12 E_1 + \tfrac12 E_0.$$
From streak 1: one throw, then even → done, odd → streak 0:
$$E_1 = 1 + \tfrac12 \cdot 0 + \tfrac12 E_0.$$

steps.title: Solve
steps.body:
First equation: $\tfrac12 E_0 = 1 + \tfrac12 E_1 \Rightarrow E_0 = 2 + E_1$.

Substitute into the second: $E_1 = 1 + \tfrac12(2 + E_1) = 2 + \tfrac12 E_1 \Rightarrow \tfrac12 E_1 = 2 \Rightarrow E_1 = 4$.

So $E_0 = 2 + 4 = 6$.

optionAnalysis.reason: $2 = 1/p$ is the expected wait for the **first** even number only.
$4 = 1/p^2$ treats "two evens" as one event of probability $\frac14$ per throw, or reports $E_1$ (the wait once one even has already been seen).
$E_0 = 6$ from the first-step equations (also $\frac1p + \frac1{p^2} = 2 + 4$).
$8$ comes from splitting the throws into disjoint pairs ($4$ pairs $\times$ 2 throws), which misses runs that straddle a pair boundary.

da-2024-da-26.shortcut: Expected throws for $k$ consecutive successes: $\frac1p + \frac1{p^2} + \dots + \frac1{p^k}$. For $k = 2$, $p = \frac12$: $2 + 4 = 6$.
pitfalls: Using 1/p² = 4 (ignores that a failure resets the streak).
Counting non-overlapping pairs (gives 8).

da-2024-da-27.approach: Match value and slope at both joints $x = \pm 2$: four linear equations in $a, b, c$. Symmetry ($|x|$ outside) forces $b = 0$ immediately.

steps.title: Continuity at x = 2 and x = −2
steps.body:
At $x = 2$: $4a + 2b + c = 2$ (value of $x$ at 2).

At $x = -2$: $4a - 2b + c = 2$ (value of $-x$ at $-2$).

Subtracting: $4b = 0 \Rightarrow b = 0$, and then $4a + c = 2$.

steps.title: Matching slopes
steps.body:
On $[-2,2]$, $f'(x) = 2ax + b$.

At $x = 2$ the right piece $x$ has slope $1$: $4a + b = 1$.

At $x = -2$ the left piece $-x$ has slope $-1$: $-4a + b = -1$.

With $b = 0$: $4a = 1 \Rightarrow a = \frac14$.

optionAnalysis.reason: $f = \frac{x^2}{4}+1$: values $2$ and slopes $\pm1$ match at both joints.
$f = \frac{x^2}{2}$ is continuous ($f(\pm2) = 2$) but $f'(2) = 2 \ne 1$ — a corner, not differentiable.
$f = 0$ on $[-2,2]$ jumps from $0$ to $2$ at $x = \pm2$ — not even continuous.

da-2024-da-27.shortcut: Outside $[-2,2]$ the function is $|x|$, which is even, so $b = 0$; the parabola must touch $y = x$ at $(2,2)$ with slope 1: $4a = 1$, $c = 2 - 4a = 1$.
pitfalls: Checking only continuity — option (B) passes it.
Using $f(-2) = -2$ instead of $-(-2) = 2$ for the left piece.
da-2024-da-27.verification: Option (A) passes all four conditions: $4\cdot\frac14 + 0 + 1 = 2$ (both joints) and $2\cdot\frac14\cdot(\pm2) = \pm1$.
